title: SAUL’S DAUGHTER MERAB HAD FIVE SONS — AND ONE WORD IN 2 SAMUEL 21 OPENS ONE OF THE BIBLE’S MOST DIFFICULT TEXTUAL QUESTIONS
paragraphs: SAUL’S DAUGHTER MERAB HAD FIVE SONS — AND ONE WORD IN 2 SAMUEL 21 OPENS ONE OF THE BIBLE’S MOST DIFFICULT TEXTUAL QUESTIONS
The Hebrew text appears to say Michal had five sons.
But another passage says Michal had no children.
And the man those five sons belonged to was married—not to Michal—but to her sister Merab.
So what happened?
Did somebody make a mistake?
Has the Bible contradicted itself?

Or are we standing at one of those rare places where God has allowed us to see something most Christians never think about—the long, human, painstaking history through which the biblical manuscripts were copied and preserved?
Stay with this one.

Because before we reach the end, five sons will die, a grieving woman will stand beneath an open sky guarding the dead, an ancient covenant will come back demanding an accounting, and a single Hebrew name will force us to ask what we really mean when we say we trust the Bible.
And somehow, beyond all of that darkness, we will find ourselves looking toward Jesus.
It begins with a famine.
Not for a few weeks.
Not for one bad agricultural season.
Three years.

The opening words of 2 Samuel 21 are heavy with desperation. Israel's ground will not give what the people need. Eventually David seeks the LORD, and the answer reaches backward into Israel's history.
There is bloodguilt connected with Saul and his house because Saul had attacked the Gibeonites.
That detail matters.

The Gibeonites were protected by an oath Israel had made generations earlier in Joshua 9. The circumstances surrounding that covenant were messy—the Gibeonites had deceived Israel—but Israel had nevertheless sworn an oath before the LORD to preserve them.
Saul's later zeal for Israel and Judah did not give him permission to treat that oath as disposable.
Religious enthusiasm does not transform disobedience into obedience.
That alone should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to become so convinced that we are defending God's interests that we begin violating God's character.
It is possible to say, “I am doing this for God,” while God is saying, “I never authorized this.”
Saul's actions were in the past.
But the consequences were not.

The Gibeonites demanded satisfaction involving seven male descendants from Saul's house. David spared Jonathan's son Mephibosheth because of his covenant with Jonathan, but seven others were handed over.
Two were sons of Rizpah.
Then comes the sentence that has caused readers, translators, scribes, and scholars to stop and look again.
The traditional Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 21:8 contains these words:
חֲמֵשֶׁת בְּנֵי מִיכַל בַּת־שָׁאוּל
ḥămēšet bənê Mîḵal bat-Šāʾûl
“The five sons of Michal, the daughter of Saul…”
There is the problem.
מִיכַל
Mîḵal.
Michal.
Not Merab.
And if you have read the earlier chapters of Samuel carefully, your mind immediately says:
Wait.
Michal?
Because 2 Samuel 6:23 had already told us that Michal, Saul's daughter, had no child to the day of her death.
And there is another difficulty.
The five sons in 2 Samuel 21:8 are connected with a man named Adriel.
But go backward to 1 Samuel 18:19.
The Hebrew says:
מֵרַב בַּת־שָׁאוּל
Mērāḇ bat-Šāʾûl.
“Merab, Saul's daughter.”
And the verse says she was given:
לְעַדְרִיאֵל הַמְּחֹלָתִי לְאִשָּׁה
ləʿAḏrîʾēl hamməḥōlāṯî ləʾiššāh
“to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife.”
There it is.
Adriel's wife was Merab.
Not Michal.
Now the tension becomes impossible to miss.
First Samuel identifies Merab as Adriel's wife.
Second Samuel 6 says Michal remained childless.
Yet the traditional Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 21:8 appears to call these five boys “the sons of Michal” in connection with Adriel.
And this is where we must resist two temptations.
The skeptic may want to shout, “Contradiction!”
The frightened Christian may want to pretend there is nothing here worth discussing.
Neither response does justice to the evidence.
Because something fascinating happened in the transmission history of this verse.

Most Hebrew manuscripts behind the Masoretic textual tradition read “Michal” here. Yet two Hebrew manuscripts, together with witnesses in the ancient Greek Septuagint tradition, support the reading “Merab.” This is why several modern English translations print “Merab” in the verse and place a textual note at the bottom explaining that the traditional Masoretic reading is “Michal.”
That footnote is not your Bible secretly confessing defeat.
It is evidence that translators are showing you their work.
They are telling you where the surviving manuscript evidence contains a variation instead of quietly pretending the variation does not exist.
And there is strong contextual reason for the reading “Merab.”
First Samuel 18:19 explicitly identifies Merab as the woman given to Adriel as his wife.
Second Samuel 6:23 explicitly reports Michal's childlessness.
Then 2 Samuel 21:8 identifies Adriel as the father connected with these five sons.
Put those pieces together, and it is easy to understand why many textual critics and modern translations regard “Merab” as the reading that best fits the historical context.
Could “Michal” nevertheless be explained?

Some interpreters historically proposed that Merab bore the children while Michal later raised them, so they could in some sense be associated with Michal. This attempts to preserve the traditional reading without making Michal their biological mother.
But Scripture never explicitly tells us that Michal adopted or raised Merab's five sons.
That distinction matters.
We should never turn a possible explanation into a revealed fact simply because it solves a difficult verse.
There is a difference between saying, “This could have happened,” and saying, “The Bible says this happened.”
It doesn't.

Another possibility—and the one reflected in many modern translations—is much simpler: at some point in the history of textual transmission, “Merab” and “Michal” became confused in this verse, while other manuscript witnesses preserved the reading “Merab.”
Christians do not need to panic at that sentence.
Ancient Scripture was copied by human hands.
Before printing presses, before photocopiers, before digital files, before cloud backups, scribes copied texts letter by letter, word by word, generation after generation.
The astonishing reality is not that manuscript variations exist.
The astonishing reality is how much evidence survives that allows scholars to identify, compare, and evaluate them.
And notice something extraordinary here.
We know there is a textual question precisely because the evidence was preserved.
Nobody successfully erased the difficulty.
Nobody standardized every surviving witness so future generations would never discover it.
The variant survived.
The evidence survived.
The earlier identification of Merab survived.
The statement concerning Michal's childlessness survived.
And now you can open an ordinary modern Bible and often find a footnote telling you about it.
That is not what concealment looks like.
That is transparency.
But if we stop with the textual problem, we will miss the human horror inside the passage.
Because these are not merely five names in a textual apparatus.
They were sons.
Five of them.
Merab's story had already contained heartbreak.
Saul had initially promised his elder daughter Merab to David, but when the appointed time came, she was instead given to Adriel the Meholathite.
Years pass.
Kings rise.
Wars are fought.
Saul dies.
David reigns.
And then the consequences of Saul's violence against the Gibeonites reach into another generation.
Seven descendants of Saul's house die.
The text is severe.
It should disturb us.
The Bible does not sanitize the brutal realities of the ancient world.
And then a woman named Rizpah does something almost impossible to forget.
Two of the dead were her sons.
The bodies remained exposed.
So Rizpah took sackcloth and spread it upon a rock.
And she stayed.
Through daylight.
Through darkness.
Through heat.
Through exhaustion.
She drove away the birds during the day.
She kept the wild animals away at night.
Imagine that mother.
Everyone else goes home.
She stays.
Night falls.
She stays.
The sun comes up again.
She stays.
Birds circle overhead.
She stays.
Animals move in the darkness.
She stays.
She cannot bring her sons back.
She cannot reverse the judgment.
She cannot rewrite yesterday.
But she can refuse to abandon their bodies.
There are griefs for which language becomes too small.
Some of you know that.
You know what it means to keep functioning after something inside you collapsed.
You answered messages.
You went to work.
You smiled when somebody greeted you.
You said, “I'm okay.”
But somewhere inside your soul, you were sitting on Rizpah's rock.
Guarding what remained of something you loved.
Maybe it was a marriage.
Maybe a child.
Maybe a parent.
Maybe your innocence.
Maybe your reputation.
Maybe a ministry.
Maybe years you cannot recover.
Maybe your relationship with God has felt like that.
You still know the songs.
You still know the verses.
You still know how Christians are supposed to answer when someone asks how you're doing.
But deep inside, you have been fighting the birds away from something that died.
And perhaps nobody noticed.
David eventually noticed Rizpah.
When he heard what she had done, something changed.
He retrieved the remains of Saul and Jonathan. The bones of those who had been executed were gathered. Saul's family finally received burial in the family tomb.
Then comes the quiet sentence:
After that, God responded to the plea for the land.
The rain came.
But there is something even deeper here.
Second Samuel 21 is about bloodguilt, covenant, judgment, grief, death, burial, and restoration.
Those themes do not end with Saul's family.
They push the Christian reader forward.
Toward another Son.
Another King.
Another death.
Another moment when bloodguilt demanded an answer.
But here we must be careful.
Jesus is not merely another victim in the story of 2 Samuel 21, and the execution of Saul's descendants is not a simple one-to-one picture of the cross.
The Gospel is greater.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ willingly gives Himself.
“No one takes it from me,” Jesus says concerning His life, “but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).
He is not dying for His own sin.
He has none.
He bears the sins of others.
Peter writes:
Paul says that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).
And suddenly the deepest scandal in Scripture becomes the doorway into grace.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because it mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
Not because justice disappeared.
Because at the cross, justice and mercy meet in Christ.
You and I have something far worse than a difficult manuscript reading.
We have a sin problem.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Manipulated.
Hidden.
Pretended.
Used religious language while protecting private rebellion.
We have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
And some of us have become extraordinarily skilled at appearing spiritually alive while secretly starving.
You can fool a congregation.
You can fool your Facebook friends.
You can fool your family.
You can sometimes fool yourself.
But you cannot fool Jesus.
And here is the Gospel:
You do not have to.
You can come into the light.
The Jesus who already knows the worst thing about you is the same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
The cross says your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
The empty tomb says God's grace is greater than your sin can defeat.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of respectable people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of dead sinners receiving life.
Guilty people receiving pardon.
Prodigals coming home.
Ashes becoming testimony.
Scandal becoming grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have spent years believing your worst chapter became your final identity.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Abandoned.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Unclean.
Unworthy.
Too far gone.
But Jesus has never needed a clean past to create a redeemed future.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a shattered relational history.
The thief beside Jesus had almost no earthly future remaining.
Grace found them anyway.
Grace does not mean your past did not happen.
Grace means your past no longer gets the authority to tell you who Christ can make you.
And maybe that is why this strange textual question in 2 Samuel 21 matters more than we first imagined.
At first we came looking for the answer to one question:
Merab or Michal?
But Scripture turned the question toward us.
What has been written across your life that you believe can never change?
What shame have you mistaken for your identity?
What hidden sin are you still defending?
What dead thing are you still guarding alone?
What covenant with sin are you protecting while asking God for rain?
Maybe the most important word you need today is not Merab.
Not Michal.
Not even David.
It is Jesus.
Ἰησοῦς.
Iēsous.
Jesus.
The One whose name announces salvation.
The One who does not merely edit your public image.
He transforms hearts.
He forgives sin.
He receives the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He gives new life.
Be honest before God.
If you need mercy, you can simply comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you cannot even explain what is happening inside you right now, comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading silently may need to discover that Christians are not people without scars. We are people whose scars no longer have the final word.
Then send this to somebody.
Not because an algorithm needs another share.
Because a person may need the truth.
Send it privately to the person who has been quietly carrying shame.
Because there will be a day when the accusation returns.
A day when your past starts speaking loudly again.

A day when you need to remember that Christianity does not require us to pretend difficult questions do not exist—and the Gospel does not require us to pretend our difficult past does not exist either.
Truth can withstand examination.
And grace can withstand your confession.
It doesn't.
Not because giving can purchase forgiveness.
It cannot.
It isn't.
Jesus purchased redemption. We cannot.
Christian giving must never be manipulated through fear, guilt, or promises that money can buy spiritual blessing.

But Scripture does teach believers to support Gospel ministry generously and willingly. Paul describes Christian giving as something decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7), and he teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for Gospel work (1 Corinthians 9:14).

Some believers may include ministry support within what they personally call their tithes and offerings; others understand New Covenant giving differently. We will not bind your conscience where Scripture does not.
Give first to God with a willing heart.
Support your local church faithfully.
Care for people in need.

Your support helps us keep producing Christ-centered biblical content, reaching struggling believers, answering difficult questions, encouraging seekers, and putting resources into the hands of people hungry for God's Word.
And there is far more waiting for those who want to go deeper.
Pray about becoming one of the people who helps carry it.
And whether you are able to support financially or not, you can still help.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the skeptic with difficult questions.
Invite the person who would never walk into a church building but might stop long enough to read about Jesus on a screen.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting on their own version of Rizpah's rock.
Guarding what remains.
Fighting through another night.
Wondering whether God still sees them.
Maybe your share reaches them.
Maybe your comment gives them courage to confess.
Maybe your testimony reminds them that grace still exists.
Maybe Scripture leads them to Christ.
And if that happens, every click becomes insignificant compared with one soul turning toward Jesus.
We began with five sons and one disputed name.
We end with a Savior whose name is not disputed by heaven.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
King.
And still calling sinners home.
Your darkest chapter may be true—but in the hands of Jesus, it does not have to be the last chapter.
